Empirical Research Plan ‑ California DSH Reform and Hospital Ownership, 1987-1995
======================================================================

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Primary design: Difference-in-Discontinuities (DiDisc) / “difference-in-RD” combined with triple differences across ownership types.

•  Regression-Discontinuity component:  Beginning in fiscal year 1990, hospitals whose low-income cost share (Medicaid + uninsured) exceeds 25 percent become eligible for large DSH per-diem payments that rise steeply above the cutoff.  This creates a discontinuous jump in the marginal profitability of caring for the indigent at the 25 % threshold.  

•  Difference-in-Differences component:  The same 25 % rule existed *only* after the 1990 reform.  Estimating the size of the discontinuity in 1990–95 and subtracting any pre-existing discontinuity in 1987-89 sweeps out fixed differences between hospitals just above and below the cutoff.

•  Triple-difference:  Interacting the DiDisc treatment with hospital ownership yields causal effects *by ownership form*.

Why appropriate?
–  The assignment variable (pre-period low-income share) is continuous and plausibly not manipulable before the policy.  
–  The policy introduces a sharp, plausibly exogenous change in incentives only for hospitals just above the 25 % threshold, giving an RD-style local experiment.
–  Using pre-reform years as an additional comparison purges any selection on unobservables correlated with the running variable, strengthening identification relative to a cross-sectional RD alone.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_ht = Post_t × Above25_h  
where Post_t = 1 for fiscal years 1990–1995 and 0 for 1987–1989;  
Above25_h = 1 if the hospital’s *baseline* (average 1987-89) low-income cost share ≥ 25 %.  
Main analysis further interacts T_ht with ownership indicators.

Control group  
Hospitals whose baseline low-income share < 25 % (specifically those in a chosen bandwidth around the cutoff) serve as controls.

Running variable and cutoff  
R_h = Baseline low-income share (%) – 25.  
Cutoff c = 0.  
Preferred bandwidth: |R_h| ≤ 5 p.p.; robustness to wider/narrower ranges.

Treatment timing  
Start of fiscal year 1990.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. No manipulation of the running variable around 25 % *before* the policy.  
   – Plausible: the rule did not exist in 1987-89, so hospitals had no incentive to bunch.

A2. Hospitals just above and below 25 % would have followed parallel trends in the absence of the DSH payments.  
   – Plausible within a narrow bandwidth; can be tested with pre-period trends and placebo discontinuities.

A3. No other policy or shock in 1990 differentially affects hospitals at the 25 % threshold.  
   – Medi-Cal rate changes applied statewide and continuously, not discontinuously at 25 %.  
   – Can check by testing for discontinuities in outcomes unlikely to be affected (e.g., number of parking spaces).

A4. Ownership status is predetermined and not shifted by the policy within the window.  
   – California hospitals seldom switch ownership type over short horizons; we verify in the data.

A5. Stable mapping from hospitals to patient ZIP codes; no sorting of low-income mothers around the threshold.  
   – We will check for discontinuities in patient demographics around the cutoff.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous coding / admission behavior could move hospitals across the 25 % line *after* 1990 (“running-variable manipulation”).  
   – Freeze Above25 using *pre-reform* shares.  
   – Report McCrary density test on baseline R_h.

T2. Differential mean reversion: hospitals slightly above 25 % may have systematically different underlying trends.  
   – Inspect pre-period outcome trends graphically and through placebo DiDisc estimates (e.g., pretend the reform happened in 1988).  
   – Include hospital fixed effects and hospital-specific linear trends in robustness checks.

T3. Spillovers: Hospitals below 25 % might lose Medicaid patients to nearby eligible hospitals, biasing estimates of utilization or health outcomes.  
   – Restrict analysis to hospitals whose nearest neighbor is > 10 miles away (robustness).  
   – At ZIP-code outcome level, instrument hospital exposure with distance-weighted eligibility to account for cross-hospital spillovers.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects estimation
library(rdrobust)    # RD validity checks
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data loading
hosp <- fread("hospital_panel_1987_1995.csv")   # one row per hospital-year
zip  <- fread("zip_birth_outcomes.csv")         # ZIP-year

# 2. Variable construction  -------------------------------------
# Baseline low-income share (average 87-89)
hosp[, li_share_base := mean(low_income_cost_share[year <= 1989]), by = hospital_id]

# Running variable
hosp[, running := li_share_base - 0.25]

# Treatment indicators
hosp[, above25 := as.integer(li_share_base >= 0.25)]
hosp[, post      := as.integer(year >= 1990)]
hosp[, treat     := above25 * post]

# Ownership dummies
hosp[, `:=`(forprofit = as.integer(owner_type=="FP"),
            nonprofit  = as.integer(owner_type=="NFP"),
            government = as.integer(owner_type=="GOV"))]

# Triple-diff interaction (FP vs. GOV baseline)
hosp[, treat_fp  := treat * forprofit]
hosp[, treat_nfp := treat * nonprofit]

# 3. Main DiDisc specification  ---------------------------------
# Outcome example: log Medicaid discharges
main <- feols(log(medicaid_discharges + 1) ~ treat + treat_fp + treat_nfp |
                hospital_id + year, data = hosp, cluster = ~hospital_id)
summary(main)

# 4. RD validity – McCrary test on baseline running variable ----
rdmc <- rddensity(hosp$running, c = 0)
summary(rdmc)

# 5. Graphical RD pre- vs post-policy ----------------------------
plotdata <- hosp[abs(running) <= 0.10,       # ±10 p.p. window
                 .(y = mean(medicaid_discharges),
                   n = .N),
                 by = .(bin = round(running, 0.01), post)]
ggplot(plotdata, aes(x = bin, y = y, color = factor(post))) +
  geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  theme_bw()

# 6. Robustness check: add hospital-specific trends -------------
robust <- feols(log(medicaid_discharges + 1) ~ treat + treat_fp + treat_nfp |
                  hospital_id[trend] + year, data = hosp, cluster = ~hospital_id)
summary(robust)
```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Economic theory suggests that raising the marginal reimbursement for Medicaid/uninsured patients should:

• Increase admission of indigent patients by *eligible* hospitals.  
• Governments (county hospitals) may have been *already* mission-oriented; marginal incentives might matter most for for-profit hospitals and least for public ones.  
Therefore I expect:  
β̂_FPorNPF > 0, with β̂_FP roughly 10-15 % increase in Medicaid discharges for hospitals just above the cutoff relative to controls over 1990-95; β̂_NFP ~ 6-10 %; β̂_GOV close to zero.  
If hospitals expand access, infant mortality in ZIP codes attached to treated FP/NFP hospitals should fall by ~0.3 deaths per 1,000 births (≈5 % of baseline).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
-------------------------------------
(Criteria adapted to DiDisc/RD)

C1: Smooth density of running variable at cutoff ….. 1  
C2: Covariates balance at cutoff in pre-period ……... 1  
C3: No visible pre-policy outcome discontinuity …… 1  
C4: Parallel pre-policy trends above/below cutoff …  1  
C5: No concurrent discontinuous policies ……………… 0.5  

Total = 4.5 / 5  → high internal validity.

------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan exploits the quasi-experimental discontinuity introduced by California’s 1990 DSH program and combines it with a pre-period difference to obtain credible, ownership-specific causal effects on hospital behavior and on health outcomes for the poor.
